channel.title: selfstore blog
channel.description: selfstore is a local-first storage library for browser apps: an automatic working copy in IndexedDB, portable encrypted ZIP backups, durable homes (a disk file, Google Drive, WebDAV, an S3 bucket) and serverless multi-device sync.

item.title: Testing a local-first app when the bugs live between sessions
item.description: A server app's test suite owns the database. A local-first app's worst bugs need an old file, a second device, a lying clock or a store that vanished overnight - and each of those can be put in a test, except one.

item.title: Supporting an app whose data you have never seen
item.description: Server-side, a bug report starts with opening the row. Local-first deletes that step and everything built on it. What replaces the database console and the log search - and the one thing you should never ask a user to send you.

item.title: What happens when the user opens a second tab
item.description: A server app serialises writes at the database. A local-first app has no such point, and every user eventually opens the app twice. The four ways that goes wrong, and the three browser primitives that fix it.

item.title: There is no password reset
item.description: A "forgot password" link is a statement about who holds the key. An app that encrypts on the client cannot offer one - so recovery has to be designed at the moment the password is chosen, not at the moment it is lost.

item.title: Browser storage is not durable storage
item.description: IndexedDB can be deleted without asking you - under disk pressure, after seven days of Safari inactivity, or with one click in the settings. What an app can actually find out about its own storage, and what it should do with the answer.

item.title: An export button is not portability
item.description: Every app has an export. Almost none of them let you leave. The difference is whether the file is readable without the software that wrote it - and there is a short test that settles it.

item.title: Schema migrations when you do not hold the database
item.description: Local-first inverts who owns the data, and with it who can run a migration. What replaces the deploy-time script - a read-time upgrade, a version that travels with the file, and a loud refusal in the other direction.

item.title: Designing an interface when the network is optional
item.description: Offline-first deletes most of the UI states a server app needs - spinners, retry toasts, optimistic rollback - and adds three smaller obligations in their place.

item.title: Why IndexedDB is the right working copy for a local-first app
item.description: A local database as the app's live state - not a server round-trip, not localStorage - and the separation between a working copy and a durable home that makes it safe.

item.title: Local-first is a security posture, not just a privacy feature
item.description: The largest breaches are server-side. Keeping one person's data on their own device removes a whole class of them - and here is exactly which class, and which threats it does not touch.

item.title: Encrypted backups in the browser, done right
item.description: What client-side encryption actually protects against, why AES-256-GCM over Argon2id, and why a format spec beats a vendor promise.

item.title: Your side project does not need a backend (yet)
item.description: An honest decision tree for when a web app actually needs a server - and how far durability, backups and multi-device sync go without one.

item.title: Multi-device sync without a sync server
item.description: Storage-as-mailbox, hybrid logical clocks and per-collection merge strategies - how deterministic convergence works when nobody runs a server.
